commonErrors: Recording withdrawal as an extensor response.
Forcing an equivocal response into flexor or extensor.
name: Plantar Response

version.label: Descriptive examination record: flexor, extensor, equivocal or no response
version.detail: Standard descriptive categories. The extensor response (Babinski sign) is upward movement of the great toe from contraction of extensor hallucis longus.

purpose: Records the response of the great toe to stimulation of the lateral sole.
intendedPopulation: Any patient undergoing neurological examination. An extensor response is expected in infants.

calculatorNotice.title: Descriptive record
calculatorNotice.message: Record each side separately. An equivocal response is better recorded as equivocal than forced into a category.

options.label: Extensor
options.detail: Great toe extends (moves up) from contraction of extensor hallucis longus; may include fanning of the other toes.

options.label: Equivocal
options.detail: Response cannot be classified confidently, e.g. withdrawal or mixed movement.

inputDefinitions.label: Side (optional)
inputDefinitions.help: Recorded for the share text only; it does not change the grade.

resultStates.label: Flexor response
resultStates.summary: Flexor plantar response at this assessment: the normal finding after infancy.
resultStates.detail: A flexor response does not exclude an upper motor neuron lesion.

resultStates.label: Extensor response (Babinski sign)
resultStates.detail: After infancy this indicates dysfunction of the corticospinal pathway; correlate with tone, reflexes and power.

resultStates.label: Equivocal
resultStates.summary: Response could not be classified confidently.
resultStates.detail: Consider repeating, or using alternative stimuli, and interpret with other signs.

resultStates.label: No response
resultStates.summary: No movement of the great toe.
resultStates.detail: Can occur with severe weakness, sensory loss or local foot problems.

clinicalContext.text: An extensor response is one of the most reliable signs of corticospinal tract dysfunction after infancy.

clinicalInsights.text: Extensor plantar response: look for associated upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, clonus, spasticity).
Compare both sides; a unilateral extensor response is particularly informative.

limitations.text: Inter-observer agreement is only moderate, particularly for equivocal responses.

limitations: Withdrawal movements can be mistaken for an extensor response.
whatItDoesNotTellYou: The level or cause of the lesion.

guideSections.what: A record of the great-toe response to stimulation of the lateral sole: flexor (normal after infancy), extensor (Babinski sign), equivocal, or no response.
guideSections.whenToUse: Every neurological examination where an upper motor neuron lesion is possible.
guideSections.howToPerform: With the patient relaxed, stroke the lateral border of the sole from heel towards the little toe, then across the ball of the foot, using a blunt object. Watch the first movement of the great toe. Test both sides.
guideSections.clinicalContext: Interpret with reflexes, tone, clonus and power.

sources.citation: van Gijn J. The Babinski reflex. Postgrad Med J. 1995;71(841):645-648.
